inserts.heading: Imagery Rescripting
inserts.html:
Imagery Rescripting

This therapy is a lot like the way I re-do trauma memories in my inner child reparenting guide. Instead of EMDR's mechanical approach. The Imagery Rescripting therapist is there with you as you explain the scene, and they step in as the ideal adult, protecting and nurturing your inner child. Then you learn to do that yourself. Because rescripting takes you back into the memory like EMDR does, the same care goes for it: stop when it's too much, and ground yourself afterward.

From a trial on 155 patients, it looks like it works on average about as well as EMDR, although that doesn't tell us if it works better or worse for you or anyone else.

inserts.heading: Pain That Won't Quit?
before: Optional High-Intensity State-Shift and Release Practices
inserts.html:
Pain That Won't Quit?

If your pain has lasted months, and a doctor has checked and found no injury or disease to explain it, there are two therapies I'd look into. In the first, Pain Reprocessing Therapy (PRT), you learn to treat the pain as a false alarm: your brain is making real pain, signaling danger where the doctors haven't found any injury. Part of how you learn it's a false alarm is by paying close attention to how the pain feels in your body, without being scared of it. As you're able, you then slowly go back to things you've been avoiding because of it, like going for walks.

Pain Reprocessing Therapy's first big trial was only in mild to moderate chronic back pain. There, 66% of the people who got four weeks of the therapy rated their pain 0 or 1 out of 10 afterward, compared to 20% of those given a placebo shot, and the gains mostly held a year later.

The second therapy is for pain that seems bound up with stressful feelings about the people in your life. Emotional Awareness and Expression Therapy (EAET) works on the feelings directly. Much of the therapy is letting out anger and other feelings you've held back, and rehearsing in role-play what you'd say to someone you've never stood up to.

And in 2024 we got evidence EAET works better than CBT, at least in veterans over age 60. 63% of them had their pain drop by at least 30% after EAET, compared to 17% with CBT. A 30% drop is a lower bar than getting your pain down to 0 or 1 out of 10, so the two trials' numbers can't be compared.

I haven't found a trial comparing EAET with PRT. So if your pain seems tied to stress or to people in your life, I'd start with the second, and otherwise with the first. I'd also ask a therapist where they trained in that therapy, and keep track of how it's going the way I describe in the last section, How I Judge Whether Any of This Is Helping.
